cards.title: Build a Company Brain as the Content Supply Chain
cards.summary: Treat a library of original long-form thinking as a compounding asset that feeds all downstream content, not a one-off piece of marketing.
cards.use_when: Deciding how to structure your store's content operation and where to invest the first content dollar before scaling volume.
steps: Identify one or two people (in-house or external) whose only job is to think deeply about your category and produce original long-form content, rather than promotional posts.
Position this output as the 'input' layer; the source argues the company brain becomes the moat because short-form, video, sales enablement and product ideas all pull from it.

Resist judging the library by a single post's direct sales attribution; the source's stated value is net-new original thinking associated with the brand over time, mined into thousands of derivative pieces.
Only invest in this if you also build the operational infrastructure to remix and distribute the library; the source says buying content without the machinery to squeeze it is a 'horrible decision.'
For ecommerce: use the library to feed product education, buying-guide copy, email streams, PDP nuance and acquisition creative, so a single deep piece spawns many store assets.
caveats: Source's '"$1M writer"' framing is illustrative, not a benchmark.
Value depends on having distribution and repurposing systems in place; content alone doesn't compound.

cards.title: Use a Minimum Volume Floor to Test Content
cards.summary: Pick an output floor high enough that content gets a fair experiment, then build the system to hit it before optimizing timing or virality.
cards.use_when: Setting your store's weekly content cadence and deciding how many assets to publish before judging what works.
steps: Adopt an explicit volume floor; the source states a minimum of five pieces per day for their agency as the baseline to give content a 'fair shot.'
Recognize this is a heuristic, not a universal rule — calibrate to your team size, budget and channel capacity.
Once volume is handled, shift attention to the higher-order question: where ideas come from (see cards on the personal language model and company brain).

Deprioritize micro-tactics the source calls irrelevant at this stage: exact posting time, paying for retweets, chasing virality; the source says none of it matters until infrastructure and library exist.
For ecommerce: pick a cadence you can sustain (e.g. X posts or short videos per week) and treat it as the floor; measure which themes drive store traffic or conversion after hitting it.
caveats: Five/day is the source's agency-specific target, not a proven benchmark; adapt to your capacity.
Quality of input still matters under high volume; don't substitute volume for original thinking.

cards.title: Get Out of Your Own Way and Publish
cards.summary: Fear of sharing a 'commodity' perspective keeps sellers from publishing; most common ideas are not risky and the real value is discovering your voice through output.
cards.use_when: Stalling on publishing store content, founder POV, or category education because the idea feels too obvious or exposing.
steps: Recognize that most feared perspectives are commodity ideas the market already agrees with (the source's example: 'the key to marketing is knowing your customer'); there is little downside to publishing them.
Treat publishing as the only way to discover the variables that make your voice, style and personality distinct — the source says you cannot find these without shipping.
Apply to ecommerce: founder POV posts, buying guides and category explainers are low-risk to publish; each one reveals which angles customers respond to.
Use early output as a diagnostic: track which published pieces drive replies, comments, replies-to-DMs or store visits, then double down.
Reframe volume as liberation, not risk — the source attributes under-publishing to self-inflicted fear rather than capability.
caveats: Doesn't apply to genuinely sensitive legal, medical or regulated claims — those still need review.
Assumes you have some baseline category knowledge to draw from.

cards.title: Build a Personal Language Model for Idea Supply
cards.summary: The volume floor only works if you have a structured source of ideas — a 'digital brain' or personal language model — feeding it.
cards.use_when: Scaling from occasional posts to a consistent content cadence and running out of things to say about your products or category.
steps: Consolidate your own thinking — notes, customer conversations, category observations, past posts — into a searchable 'digital brain.'
Design it as the input layer that answers 'where are the ideas coming from?' so AI can help remix and produce without inventing substance.
Keep the source material original and first-person (your perspective, your customers' language) so remixed output stays differentiated.
Use AI at the remix/production stage, not the ideation stage; the source frames AI as infrastructure on top of a human-generated library.

For ecommerce: seed the library with customer questions, reviews, support tickets and product-use observations — this creates a near-infinite supply of on-brand content angles tied to real shopping behavior.
caveats: Requires ongoing capture discipline; a stale library produces stale output.
AI remixing without a strong source library tends toward generic commodity content.

cards.title: Treat Content as Data You Own and License
cards.summary: Language, writing and content libraries are data assets; their value depends on whether you have the infrastructure to mine and leverage them.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to buy, license, or commission content assets (writer catalogs, data sets) to fuel your store's marketing.
steps: Recognize the source's framing: libraries of words and crystallized thinking are data you can leverage the same way you leverage structured data.
Before acquiring any content asset, audit whether you have the operational infrastructure to scale, slice and distribute it; the source says poor infrastructure makes the acquisition a bad deal.
For ecommerce, treat your own accumulated content (past campaigns, product copy, customer emails) as an owned data asset and mine it for reuse before paying for external libraries.
Note the source's example of Micro One buying Spirit Airlines data as an illustration of data value being determined by leverage potential, not intrinsic worth.
Build the 'squeeze the juice' machinery first — repurposing workflows, AI tools, distribution channels — so any content input produces many outputs.
caveats: Source's data-acquisition examples are illustrations, not verified purchase prices or outcomes.
'Content is data' is a strategic framing, not a legal position on usage rights.

cards.title: Fund a Deep Thinker Over Promotional Output
cards.summary: The source's strongest opinion: the best marketing spend is hiring a thoughtful writer to produce original long-form thinking, not more promotional content.
cards.use_when: Allocating content budget or hiring for content and deciding whether to prioritize promotional copy or original category thinking.
steps: Attach the source's opinion clearly: the best money a large company could spend is paying a smart journalist or nonfiction writer to think deeply about the industry and write long form — their only job.
Explicitly avoid what the source warns against: making output super promotional; the value is net-new original thinking associated with the company, not a single piece driving all sales.
For ecommerce: instead of another round of discount announcements, hire or commission someone to write deeply about your category's problems, materials, use cases, or buying decisions.
Then connect that library to store assets (PDP context, email education, acquisition hooks) so the thinking reaches shoppers.
Judge this role over a long horizon — the source positions it as building a library leveraged for a long period, not immediate conversion.
caveats: This is the source's opinion, not a universal rule; it suits brands with budget and patience.
Long-form original thinking is hard to attribute to direct sales; don't measure it like a paid ad.

cards.title: Separate Infrastructure From Idea Input
cards.summary: Posting volume is infrastructure; the harder question is the quality of input flowing into it — treat them as two distinct decisions.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing why store content isn't working — is it cadence/distribution or is it the underlying ideas?
steps: Split the problem: (1) do you have the systems to ship at your target volume, and (2) do you have a supply of high-quality original input?
Solve infra first — scheduling, repurposing, AI-assisted production — so volume is not the bottleneck.
Once infra exists, the source says the question is 'what is the input?'; if posting daily, where are ideas pulled from?
For ecommerce, this prevents the common failure of shipping more generic deal posts; a content library tied to customer questions and category insight supplies differentiated input.
Route outputs from the input library into multiple channels (email, PDP, social, paid creative) via the infra layer, so one idea reaches shoppers in several formats.
caveats: Source treats this as two layers but doesn't prescribe specific tooling.
Without a genuine input supply, better infra just produces more commodity content faster.

cards.title: Let Robots Repeat, Humans Originate
cards.summary: Assign AI the repeating/remixing work and keep humans on original thinking — this division is the source's core division of labor.
cards.use_when: Designing how much of your store's content production to automate versus keep human-authored.
steps: Define the human role as creating the highest-quality input (original ideas, deep thinking, distinctive voice).
Assign AI and systems the repetition: slicing long content into shorts, generating automated video, producing volume across formats.
Keep a human-curated source library as the reference so AI remixes stay anchored to original substance rather than inventing generic claims.
For ecommerce: a single deep category or product-use article can be chopped into email snippets, PDP FAQ lines, ad hooks and short video scripts via automated remix.
Review remixed output for brand voice and factual accuracy before it reaches shoppers, since AI is doing the repeating, not the origination.
caveats: Requires a genuine input library; without it, AI output drifts generic.
No specific AI tools are named; verify current tool interfaces before committing to a workflow.

cards.title: Prioritize Library Over Virality Tactics
cards.summary: The source dismisses tactical virality chasing in favor of a valuable content library pulled from repeatedly over time.
cards.use_when: Deciding where to spend limited content effort — micro-optimization versus building a reusable library for your store.
steps: List the micro-tactics the source calls irrelevant: exact posting time, chasing virality, paying for retweets — none matter if the library and infra are absent.
Redirect that effort into producing and organizing a library you can pull from over a long period.
For ecommerce: instead of optimizing one post's timing, build evergreen category content you can resurface seasonally or reuse in email and paid creative.
Measure library value by how many downstream assets it feeds and how long it stays usable, not by a single post's reach.
Accept the source's framing that this is 'timely versus timeless' — build the timeless asset.
caveats: Timing and platform tactics aren't worthless; the source's claim is relative priority when the library is missing.
For very small stores, a modest library may be more effort than a few well-placed posts.

cards.title: Expect Media Components in Brand Strategy
cards.summary: The source observes large companies building media arms; for ecommerce this maps to owning category narrative, not just posting.
cards.use_when: Setting a long-term content direction for your brand and deciding whether to invest in owned media rather than relying on ad spend.
steps: Recognize the source's cited trend: large companies realizing they need a media component (e.g., OpenAI's podcast acquisition cited in the source).
For ecommerce, treat owned content as a channel you control, similar to how a brand would own its category's conversation.
Feed this media component from the same company brain/library rather than producing disconnected one-off pieces.
Use the media output to build brand association with original thinking, which the source says is the real marketing mechanism — not each piece's direct sales.
Verify current platform and partnership details before copying any specific company example, since the source references specific acquisitions that may change.
caveats: Cited company examples (OpenAI, Salesforce, Slack, Airbnb, Spirit Airlines/Micro One) are illustrative, not case studies with published results.
Media investment is a long-horizon play, not a direct-response tactic.

cards.title: Assess Content Assets by Leverage, Not Intrinsic Value
cards.summary: The source argues a content asset's value is determined by how well you can leverage it, not by what it is.
cards.use_when: Evaluating whether to buy, license or commission content (writer catalogs, creator libraries, data sets) for your store.
steps: Before acquiring content, write down the specific infrastructure you'll use to distribute and monetize it (email list, social channels, SEO pages, paid creative).
If you lack that infrastructure, the source says the acquisition becomes 'a horrible decision' regardless of asset quality.
For ecommerce, prefer content assets you can tie directly to your products, categories or customer questions so leverage is obvious.
Model the number and type of downstream assets a library can produce, not just its standalone quality.
Use the Spirit Airlines/Micro One example only as the source's illustration that the same asset looks cheap to a seller and valuable to a leveraged buyer — not as a validated price or outcome.
caveats: No verified financial details or outcomes for the cited acquisition.
Leverage potential depends on channels and tools, which the source doesn't specify.

input.text:
d it was comical to me. ghostwriting for so many people where I would have a client be like, I'm really afraid of putting my perspective out there. And their perspective is like the key to marketing is knowing your customer. I'm like, there's nothing, there's nothing to be afraid of. You are literally repeating a commodity idea that most of the planet agrees with. Like, and so a lot of these are self-inflicted issues. And the, the whole key is like getting out of your own way and hitting publish so that you can discover what these variables are. You know, what makes your personality? What makes your writing style? What makes your voice? The other piece of that is, generally speaking, people are under publishing, like the volume of content that they're putting out is lower than they can actually do. I was having this conversation with our agency, actually. And LCA literally works with the biggest companies on the planet building their new products. So there's, as you can imagine, in the AI world, as you can imagine, that team has just an incredible data set and incredible knowledge base around what's working and what's not. and there's so much content that they could be putting out.

 And they put out some content here and there, but I think one of the things we were talking about is how do we ship a minimum of five pieces of content a day? And what does that look like? What systems do we need in place? And we could use AI in that process, but what systems do we need in place for that to happen? Because if we're not posting five pieces of content per day, I don't believe we're giving it a fair shot. I would agree. And I would say that it's important for people to remember that that is in many ways, that is the baseline expectation now. And that is just the infrastructure. The question on top of that is, what is the input? If you're posting five times a day, like, where are you pulling the ideas from? Goes back to, well, you need a digital brain, you need a personal language model. Like, where is it all coming from? And the same way, I know you're aware of the trend, you know, you see like OpenAI acquired that podcast, TBPN, and there's a huge move to these like large companies realizing they need a media component. I think that it might be idealistic, but I think that some of the best marketing money that any Fortune 500 company could spend would be plucking really thoughtful journalists and nonfiction writers in relevant or tangentially relevant fields and being like, you have one job. We're going to pay you a fat salary and your only job is to think deeply about our industry and write long form content about it. That's it. Because what's really happening is it's not that like that individual piece of writing is the silver bullet and that's going to drive all the sales and they make it all super promotional. What's really happening is you have a very smart person who's paid to think deeply about a topic, hopefully over time creating net new original thinking and ideas that get associated with the company. And that library of content feeds the infrastructure. It feeds your whole supply chain. It's like just to make it visceral, Greg, it's like imagine you were like, cool, I'll pay you a million bucks a year. I want you to do nothing but think deeply about the future of AI and technology and the implications it's going to have on product building. And I just want you to build like a world class long form content library that all of our different departments can pull from. The robots do the repeating. We can pluck short form. We could turn it into automated videos like all the infrastructure. I just want you to create the highest quality input. Now, imagine if Salesforce did that with like a Pulitzer Prize winning journalist or Slack did that. I think that the leverage you get out of that is so it's so hard for people to wrap their heads around. And they're so focused on the minutia of like we got I post five times a day and what time of day and how do we go viral and can we pay for retweets and like all none of it matters. None of it matters. What matters is you have the infrastructure and you have a very valuable content library that you pull from and leverage for a long period of time Yeah I mean that why people are starting to say the company brain is the moat Yes. Right? Because if I hired you, Cole, and you're adding to this company brain and it's getting more and more valuable and I can use robots to go and slice and dice it a million ways, I know it sounds crazy to pay someone a million dollars, But it's not that crazy if the value from that million dollars is thousands of pieces of content. It's improving workflows. It's helping with the product. It's pretty insane, right? And that's why you're starting to see actually companies spend millions of dollars, tens of millions of dollars. And I think it will be hundreds of millions of dollars on data licensing or buying data. I saw Micro One buying data, Spirit Airlines data, for I think millions of dollars. And why? Because they're going to use that data. They're going to mine that data. And I think that's where everything is going. That's exactly it. It's just people understand this idea more in technology. They go, oh, we acquired a company that just filed for bankruptcy and we bought all their data. and everyone's like, yep, I instantly understand the value. The reality is language and writing and libraries of content are data. And you are buying groupings of words, you are buying ideas, you are buying crystallized thinking that you can leverage the same way you leverage data. Yeah, it's funny because I bet the Spirit Airlines people are probably like, ha ha ha ha, I can't believe they bought our data for millions of dollars. Idiots. and the Micro One people are like, ha ha ha ha, I can't believe they sold us the data for so cheap. Yeah, well, it's always a question of, it's actually not really the value of those assets in and of themselves. The question is, how do you leverage it? If you're a company and you buy some writer's entire catalog and library of content, and then you don't have the operational infrastructure to scale it and squeeze all the juice out of it, then that was a horrible decision because you're not able to do what you should do with it.
